nameStory: The Canada sand-spurry gets its name from its original discovery and classification in Canadian coastal regions, though it's found throughout northern North America. The "sand-spurry" part describes both its habitat preference for sandy shores and its spurry-like appearance - spurry being an old English name for small, delicate plants with narrow leaves that seem to "spur" out from the stem.
description: Canada sand-spurry is a small annual herb that hugs the ground along northern coastlines. This delicate plant grows up to 10 inches tall with slender stems lined with fleshy, needle-like leaves. Its tiny white or pale pink flowers bloom in small clusters at stem tips, creating a modest but charming display. The entire plant has a succulent-like quality that helps it survive in salty, harsh coastal conditions.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Fleshy, linear leaves up to 1.8 inches long that feel thick and slightly rubbery between your fingers, like tiny succulent needles arranged along the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny five-petaled flowers, white to pale pink, with pointed green sepals that are often longer than the oval petals themselves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads along the ground with slender stems, rarely exceeding 10 inches in height

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found in wet, salty areas like beaches and salt marshes where few other plants can survive

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Shiny reddish-brown seeds contained in small capsules that split open when ripe, often visible with a hand lens

habitat: In New England, Canada sand-spurry thrives in coastal salt marshes, sandy beaches, and brackish estuaries from Maine down to northern Massachusetts and New York. Look for it in wet, often flooded areas where salt spray reaches, growing alongside saltmarsh asters, sea lavender, and glasswort. It prefers the muddy-sandy edges of tidal pools and salt pannes where the soil stays consistently moist and salty.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes of fleshy leaves in late spring, beginning their rapid growth cycle in the warming coastal soils.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs throughout summer with tiny white to pink flowers appearing continuously. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and distinctive succulent leaves are present.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and split open, releasing the characteristic shiny reddish-brown seeds. Plants begin to decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, Canada sand-spurry dies completely with the first hard frosts, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the sandy soil.

funFact: Canada sand-spurry can actually filter and concentrate salt from seawater through its roots and store it in special cells in its fleshy leaves, essentially turning itself into a living salt-processing plant that would make ocean desalination engineers jealous!
confusionNotes: The three sand-spurries in New England can be tricky to tell apart, but Canada sand-spurry is the most northern and coastal species. Red sand spurrey has pinker flowers and grows in drier sandy soils inland, while saltmarsh sand spurry is larger and more robust. Think "Canada = coast" to remember this one stays closest to the ocean.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's only Canadian, this plant is actually found along both North American coasts from Alaska to California in the west, and from maritime Canada down to New York in the east. The "Canadian" name simply reflects where botanists first formally described it.
compareHints: Canada sand-spurry is the most cold-tolerant and northern of the three sand-spurries in New England. Unlike red sand spurrey, which grows in dry sandy areas inland, Canada sand-spurry requires wet, salty conditions and has fleshier leaves. Compared to saltmarsh sand spurry, it's smaller and more delicate, with thinner stems and typically paler flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red sand spurrey differs from its relative saltmarsh sand spurrey by growing in dry sandy areas rather than salt marshes, and having smaller flowers with less fleshy leaves.
Unlike Red Sand Spurrey which has distinctly pink flowers and grows in dry, non-salty areas, Saltmarsh Sand Spurry has white to very pale pink flowers and requires salty conditions.
